Viking Health Atlas

A cemetery, a tooth, a genome, and a piece of wood answer different historical questions. Start with the sample.

Ribe

c. AD 800–1800; separate period groups · Across periods

Sample
943 adult skeletons across three periods
Evidence
Osteology

What the record supports

The study compares adult age-at-death patterns across Viking, medieval, and post-medieval cemetery samples.

Limits of interpretation

943 is the combined sample, not the Viking-only denominator. Adult skeletal mean age at death is not life expectancy at birth. Burial selection, age estimation, and changing population structure matter.

Evidence and sources

  • A millennium of population change in pre-modern Danish RibeReviewed abstract · Source date: 2019

Three samples, three different questions.

These studies cannot be pooled into a single measure of Viking health.

Birka — grave Bj 581 10th century AD

10th century AD · Viking Age

Sample
1 individual, with two DNA samples
Evidence
Ancient DNA

What the record supports

Genomics supported a female sex estimate for the person in grave Bj 581; the burial contained martial equipment.

Limits of interpretation

The study reports no pathological or traumatic injuries. Genomic sex and the interpretation of a social role do not establish whether an individual fought in battle. One burial supplies no population prevalence.

Evidence and sources

  • Hedenstierna-Jonson et al. A female Viking warrior confirmed by genomicsReviewed methods and discussion · Source date: 2017-09-08
Varnhem 10th–12th centuries AD

10th–12th centuries AD · Across periods

Sample
171 individuals; 133 permanent and 38 deciduous/mixed dentitions
Evidence
Dental examination

What the record supports

83 of 171 individuals had caries (49%). Among the permanent dentitions, 424 of 3,293 examined teeth were affected (13%).

Limits of interpretation

The excavation and jaw-preservation criteria select the sample. These are different denominators, and the cemetery extends beyond the conventional Viking Age. Tooth loss can bias observed caries prevalence.

Evidence and sources

  • Bertilsson et al. Caries prevalence and other dental pathological conditions in Vikings from Varnhem, SwedenReviewed full text · Source date: 2023-12-13
L’Anse aux Meadows AD 1021: dated wood-cutting activity

AD 1021: dated wood-cutting activity · Viking Age

Sample
3 worked wood pieces used for exact dating
Evidence
Archaeological dating

What the record supports

A cosmic-ray radiocarbon marker places the cutting of the studied wood in AD 1021.

Limits of interpretation

These are wood samples, not human remains. The date documents activity at the site; it does not establish a disease introduction or a complete occupation interval.

Evidence and sources

  • Kuitems et al. Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021Reviewed article · Source date: 2021-10-20
Eastern Settlement, Greenland Norse occupation through the 15th century

Norse occupation through the 15th century · Later Norse

Sample
No human skeletal sample in this model
Evidence
Environmental model

What the record supports

A sea-level model evaluates coastal flooding as a possible contributor to later Norse settlement abandonment.

Limits of interpretation

The geographic marker locates the settlement region, not a sampled patient or exact model cell. Environmental pressure, epidemic mortality, and a sole cause of abandonment are separate claims.

Evidence and sources

  • Borreggine et al. Sea-level rise in Southwest Greenland as a contributor to Viking abandonmentReviewed abstract · Source date: 2023
Ridgeway Hill, Weymouth Viking Age; see dating discussion in excavation report

Viking Age; see dating discussion in excavation report · Viking Age

Sample
Minimum number depends on the skeletal inventory; consult the report
Evidence
Mortuary archaeology

What the record supports

An excavated mass burial documents decapitation and a highly selected episode of violent death.

Limits of interpretation

A mass execution is not a representative cemetery sample. The identity of the group and historical event attribution require separate arguments.

Evidence and sources

  • Loe et al. Given to the Ground: A Viking Age Mass Grave on Ridgeway Hill, WeymouthReviewed repository description and introductory chapter · Source date: 2014
